newsitem.title: USA: UTC reports better-than-expected profit, stock jumps.
newsitem.headline: UTC reports better-than-expected profit, stock jumps.

text.p: United Technologies Corp. Thursday reported better-than-expected fourth-quarter and full-year earnings and signalled it expected similar growth in 1997, sending its stock sharply higher.

The maker of Otis elevators, Carrier air conditioners, Sikorsky helicopters and Pratt & Whitney jet engines said sales grew in all its businesses for the quarter and year, except for flight systems because of fewer helicopter deliveries to the federal government.

The Hartford, Conn.-based company said net income jumped 22 percent to $229 million, or 87 cents a share, in the quarter, from $187 million, or 71 cents a share, in the 1995 period. Sales grew 2.8 percent to $6.14 billion from $5.97 billion.
Analysts had forecast profits of 83 cents a share for the quarter on average, according to First Call, which tracks estimates.
"The operating performance of the company was terrific across all lines of business," said Joe Campbell, aerospace analyst at Lehman Brothers. "The whole company did well."

United Tech's stock jumped $4.25 to $70.75, a new 52-week high, in active trading on the New York Stock Exchange, and helped to send the Dow Jones industrial average up more than 50 points though the index later gave back some of the gain.

"We had another excellent year in 1996, with 21 percent earnings per share growth and continued strong cash generation. We expect to carry that momentum into 1997 and beyond," Chief Executive Officer George David said in a statement.
The company did not elaborate on the earnings momentum but analysts said investors believe the company will continue to boost profit margins.

"If you could take this huge company with $23 billion in sales and turn it around and make it 50 percent more profitable, that's why folks get excited about the upside," said Nick Heymann, analyst at NatWest Securities.
He noted that the company's profit margins of 8.6 percent were respectable but lagged those of some competitors such as General Electric Co., with margins closer to 15 percent.

Pratt & Whitney's operating profit rose 18 percent in the quarter on cost reductions and higher service and other revenue, the company said. Flight systems' operating profit grew 12 percent despite lower sales.

Analysts also said Boeing Co.'s decision this week to halt development of a superjumbo 747 jetliner could free up $400 million Pratt & Whitney had planned to spend on engine development for the plane in a venture with GE.
"The question is what do they do with all that extra money?" said one analyst.
Profits at Otis, the world's biggest maker of elevators and escalators, were flat in the quarter as charges for job cuts in Europe and foreign currency translations offset higher revenues.
Operating profit at Carrier rose 4 percent in what is a seasonally weak quarter on a good performance in all regions.
Fourth-quarter profits included a $78 million pretax gain from the sale of a steering wheel business that was more than offset by charges in automotive and other units.
Excluding the gain on the steering wheel business and other items, profit fell in the automotive unit in the quarter.
For the full year, earnings grew 21 percent to $906 million, or $3.45 a share, from $750 million, or $2.85 a share, in 1995. Sales rose 3.1 percent to $23.51 billion from $22.80 billion.
